title: Managing the language barrier in international business

paragraphs.text: Multinational business enterprises commonly have branches and customers in many different countries, some or all of which operate in a different language. Language therefore needs to be managed as a corporate asset. There are several options available to multinational companies (MNCs) for dealing with language barriers, and alleviating the potentially serious problems they create.

The simplest option is to rely on the language of the parent company. Widespread though this strategy is, however, it is fatally flawed. It makes no allowance for the growing trend of linguistic nationalism, whereby buyers in some regions assert their right to work in the local language. And total reliance on a single language puts a company at risk in other ways. Contracts, rules and legislation are invariably written in the local language, and a company unable to operate in that language is vulnerable.

Another improvised approach to language taken by MNCs is to rely on what has been termed ‘Functional Multilingualism’ (Hagen, 1999). Essentially what this means is muddling through, relying on a mix of languages, pidgins and gestures to communicate by whatever means the parties have at their disposal. Ina social context such a shared effort might be considered an aid to the bonding process, with the frustration of communication being regularly punctuated by moments of absurdity and humor. However, as the basis for business negotiations it appears very hit-and-miss. And yet Hagen’s recent study suggests that as much as 16% of international business transactions are conducted in a ‘cocktail of languages’. Functional Multilingualism shares the same defects as reliance on a lingua franca” and increases the probability of misunderstandings.

A more rational and obvious response to the language barrier is to employ external resources such as translators and interpreters, and certainly there are many excellent specialists in these fields. However, such a response is by no means a perfect solution. For a start, these services can be very expensive, with a top simultaneous interpreter commanding daily rates as high as a partner in an international consulting company. Secondly, any good translator or interpreter will insist that, to be fully effective, they must understand the context of the subject matter. However, this is not always possible. In some cases it is prohibited by the complexity or specialization of the topic, and sometimes by lack of preparation time, but most often the obstacle is the reluctance of the parties to explain the wider context to an ‘outsider’. Another problem is that unless there has been considerable pre-planning between the interpreter and his/her * lingua franca: a language that is adopted as a common language between speakers whose native languages are different. clients, it is likely that there will be ambiguity and cultural overtones in the source messages the interpreters have to work with. They will endeavor to provide a hi-fidelity translation, but in this circumstance they have to use initiative and guesswork, which injects a potential source of misunderstanding into the proceedings. Finally, while a good interpreter will attempt to convey not only the meaning but also the correct emphasis of any communication, there can be no doubt that there is a loss of rhetorical power when communications go through a third person. So, in situations requiring negotiation, persuasion, humor, etc, the use of an interpreter is a poor substitute for direct communication.

The immediate and understandable reaction to any skills shortage in a business is to consider personnel development, and certainly the language-training industry is well developed, offering programs at almost every level and in numerous languages. However, without doubting the value of language training, no company should be deluded into believing that it will be assured of success. Training in most companies is geared to the economic cycle. When times are good, money is invested in training. When companies have financial difficulties, training is one of the ‘unnecessary luxuries’ that have to be cut from the budget. In a study conducted across four European countries (Hagen, 1999), nearly twice as many companies said they needed language training in the coming years as had actually provided it in the past years. This disparity between intentions and practice underlines the problems of relying upon training for language skills. Unless the company is totally committed to sustaining the strategy, even through bad times, it will fail.

One notable and committed leader in the field of language training has been the Volkswagen Group. They have developed a language program over many years, and in many respects can be regarded as a model of how to manage language resources professionally. However, the Volkswagen approach underlines the fact that language training has to be considered a long-term strategy rather than a short-term, tactical solution. In their system, to progress from ‘basics’ to ‘communications competence’ in a language requires the completion of six levels, each one of which requires approximately 90 hours of classroom tuition, supported by many more hours of self-study, spread over a 6-9 month period. The completion of each stage is marked by a post-stage achievement test, which is a pre-requisite for continued training. So even this professionally managed program requires a minimum of three years of fairly intensive study of a language to produce accountants, engineers, buyers or salespeople able to work effectively in it. Clearly, companies intending to pursue this route need to do so with realistic expectations and with the intention of sustaining the program over many years. Apart from refresher courses for people who were previously fluent in a foreign language, training cannot be considered a quick fix.
